Interpolate values from one set of polygons onto another by area

Source: R/extendr-wrappers.R
ga_interpolate_aw.Rd

Moves values that describe the polygons of x onto the polygons of to, sharing each value out by the area the two overlap. This matches sf::st_interpolate_aw().

Usage

ga_interpolate_aw(
  x,
  values,
  to,
  extensive,
  include_non_intersected = FALSE,
  allocate_total = FALSE,
  na_rm = FALSE,
  weights = NULL
)

Arguments

x

a GeoArrow polygon array that the values describe

values

the values of x, one row per row of x or a single row for all of them: a numeric vector or float array, or a data frame, list, or struct array of numeric columns

to

a GeoArrow polygon array to interpolate onto

extensive

TRUE to interpolate a column by preserving its total, FALSE to preserve its mean; length 1 or one per column of values

include_non_intersected

whether to divide an intensive column by the whole area of each target rather than the part the sources cover

allocate_total

whether to divide an extensive column by the part of each source the targets cover rather than its whole area

na_rm

whether to drop each source with a null in any column of values

weights

the weight of each row of to, to share extensive values out by in place of area, or NULL

Value

a float64 array of the same length as to, or a struct array of float64 columns when values is a table

Details

Areal interpolation needs to know how each value relates to the area it describes, which you state with extensive. For a spatially extensive value, such as a count of people, ga_interpolate_aw() gives each target the share of the value in proportion to the area it takes from the source, so it preserves the total. For a spatially intensive value, such as a density, ga_interpolate_aw() gives each target the mean of the values it overlaps, weighted by area, so it preserves the mean.

With a the area that source i shares with target j, ga_interpolate_aw() returns the sum over i of v[i] * a / A[i] for an extensive column, where A[i] is the area of the source, and of v[i] * a / B[j] for an intensive column, where B[j] is the area of the target that the sources cover. allocate_total = TRUE takes A[i] as the area of the source that the targets cover, so ga_interpolate_aw() hands out all of each value even where the targets leave part of its source uncovered, as tobler's area_interpolate() does by default. include_non_intersected = TRUE takes B[j] as the whole area of the target, as sf's argument of that name does.

With weights, ga_interpolate_aw() shares each source out by weight rather than by area, as sf does for dasymetric mapping. It spreads the weight of each target over its overlaps by area, then gives each overlap the fraction of its source's weight that it holds. ga_interpolate_aw() takes weights for extensive columns only.

ga_interpolate_aw() measures planar area, so project geographic coordinates first. It reads polygons, multipolygons, and boxes, and treats any other geometry as covering nothing. It counts a source as overlapping a target only when their intersection has area, so it ignores polygons that share just an edge.

ga_interpolate_aw() returns null for a target that no source overlaps, and for a target that a source with a null value overlaps. With na_rm = TRUE, it first drops each source with a null in any column, as sf's na.rm does. When values is a table, ga_interpolate_aw() returns a struct array that is null in each row no source overlaps.

References

Pebesma, E., Fleischmann, M., Parry, J., et al. (2025). Spatial data science languages: commonalities and needs. Journal of Spatial Information Science, 31, 119–144. doi:10.5311/JOSIS.2025.31.462

See also

Other aggregate: ga_collect_agg(), ga_unary_union()

Examples

nc <- sf::st_transform(
  sf::read_sf(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf")),
  32119
)
counties <- geoarrow::as_geoarrow_array(sf::st_geometry(nc))
cells <- ga_make_grid(counties, n = c(10, 5))

# births are a count, so the cells keep the state's total
births <- ga_interpolate_aw(counties, nc$BIR74, cells, extensive = TRUE)
sum(as.vector(births), na.rm = TRUE) / sum(nc$BIR74)
#> [1] 1

# a count and a rate together, each with its own support
both <- data.frame(births = nc$BIR74, sids_rate = nc$SID74 / nc$BIR74)
out <- ga_interpolate_aw(counties, both, cells, extensive = c(TRUE, FALSE))
head(na.omit(as.data.frame(out)))
#>        births   sids_rate
#> 6   531.58653 0.004002972
#> 7  4837.74162 0.003674742
#> 8  6487.63049 0.002492565
#> 14   30.75959 0.001021711
#> 15 2477.34775 0.005111840
#> 16 8683.01518 0.003622510
